text: Millimeter wave communication (mmWave) is an important enabler for 5G applications that require multi-gigabit data rates and low latency, such as cooperative perception, high-resolution map distribution and remote driving. However, mmWave connections are very sensitive to blocking, mobility and beam misalignments, and most existing studies evaluate these effects isolated on the physical or link layer and provide only a limited insight into the performance that applications actually experience. This paper presents an evaluation framework for end-to-end 5G mmWave communication in vehicle environments. The framework combines a network simulator that implements a full 5G protocol stack, including beam management, handover, radio access and core networks, as well as transport layer protocols, with a microscopic traffic simulator and a geometric channel model that captures dynamic blockages through surrounding vehicles and buildings. The application models enable the measurement of end-to-end measurements such as latency, throughput, parcel delivery ratio and age of information under realistic traffic conditions. Based on the framework, we evaluate representative networked vehicle applications in urban and highway scenarios with different base station densities, traffic loads and deployment options, including multi-access edge computing. The results show that while mmWave connections can meet the throughput requirements of bandwidth-intensive applications under line of sight conditions, they introduce frequent blockage and transfer events that can violate the requirements of safety-critical services. TCP-based applications are particularly affected, with a sharp decrease in throughput in connection interruptions. We also show that denser station deployment, multi-connectivity and edge computing significantly improve reliability and latency. The framework forms the basis for the design and evaluation of mmWave-based vehicle networks.

text: Oakland Ski Club is one of the oldest recreational ski clubs in Northern California. It was founded by ski enthusiasts from the San Francisco Bay Area, especially Oakland and the surrounding East Bay, during the early growth of recreational skiing in the Sierra Nevada in the first half of the twentieth century. The club is known for owning and operating its own lodge in the Sierra, in the Donner Summit area near Soda Springs, along the old Highway 40 corridor west of Lake Tahoe. Note: There is limited information about small private clubs like this, and details such as the exact founding year and membership numbers vary between sources. If you need accurate facts for an assignment, it is best to confirm them with the club's own website or local historical sources (see suggestions at the end). ## History and background In the 1920s and 1930s, skiing in California changed from a practical means of winter travel to a popular sport. The completion of the transcontinental railway and later improvements of the motorway via the Donnerpass made the Sierra accessible to the inhabitants of the Bay Area. Groups of enthusiasts started to form clubs so they could pool resources, organize excursions and build or rent lodges near the slopes. The Oakland Ski Club was part of this movement. Like several of his contemporaries, such as the lodges of the Sierra Club and other Bay Area ski clubs, it built a member-run lodge near Donner Summit, which was one of the most important ski hubs in Northern California due to its heavy snowfall and railway and road access. In the Donner Summit area there were also some of the earliest ski lifts and ski schools in the West of the United States. ## How the club works The association works according to a cooperative, member-based model that is typical of traditional ski clubs: - **Membership:** Members pay fees and often a one-time start fee. In return, you will get access to the lodge at discounted prices. - **Lodge:** The lodge offers dormitory style or shared rooms, a shared kitchen and dining area, and common spaces such as a fireplace lounge. It allows members to stay near nearby resorts such as Sugar Bowl, Donner Ski Ranch, Boreal and Soda Springs. - **Work parties:** Members often contribute volunteer work, such as cleaning, repairs and preparing the lodge for the winter, which helps keep costs low. - **Guests:** Many clubs of this type allow members to bring guests, and some rental places for the public or groups when available. ## Activities While skiing and snowboarding are the focus in winter, clubs such as the Oakland Ski Club often organize: - Group skiing and carpooling from the Bay Area - social events, dinners and holiday meetings - cross-country and snowshoe hikes - summer activities such as hiking, mountain biking and sea tours, as the lodge can be used all year round # Meaning The Oakland Ski Club is a good example of how ordinary residents of the Bay Area have contributed to making skiing accessible before the rise of large commercial resorts. The lodges run by the members reduced the cost of a ski weekend and created close communities, many of which have existed for generations, with children and grandchildren still affected by early members. For a college assignment, the club could be in the context of: - The History of Leisure Skiing in California - The Role of Voluntary Associations and Associations in American Social Life - Regional History of the Donner Summit Area ## Where to find more information - The official website of the association, which usually contains history, lodge details and membership information - The **Donner Summit Historical Society**, which publishes articles on the ski history and lodges of the region - Local newspaper archives, such as the *Oakland Tribune* - books on Californian ski history, such as those on the development of Sugar Bowl and the Donner Summit ski resorts These sources will help you confirm certain data and details before you specify them.
